passages.source_text: κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην Οὐ δοκεῖ σοι οὖν φιλάνθρωπος εἶναι κἂν ἡ ξενοδόχος, ξένην ἣν οὐκ ἠπίστατο εὐεργετήσασα; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἐλεήμονα μὲν αὐτὴν εἰπεῖν ἐπίσταμαι, φιλάνθρωπον δὲ οὐ τολμῶ λέγειν, ἅτε δὴ οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν φιλότεκνον· ὑπ’ ὠδίνων γὰρ καὶ ἀνατροφῆς στέργειν πέπεισται. ὡς καὶ ὁ ἐρῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συνηθείας κολακεύεται καὶ εὐνῆς καὶ ὁ φίλος ὑπὸ τῆς ἀμοιβῆς: οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἐλεῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συμφορᾶς. πλὴν ἐγγὺς ὁ ἐλεήμων τῷ φιλανθρώπῳ, ὅτι ἄνευ τοῦ τι θηρᾶσθαι λαβεῖν εὐεργετεῖν πείθεται. πλὴν οὕτω φιλάνθρωπός ἐστιν. κἀγὼ ἔφην Ἐπὶ ποίαις οὖν πράξεσιν φιλάνθρωπος εἶναί τις δύναται; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο Ἐπεὶ ὁρῶ σε γλιχόμενον ἀκοῦσαι τί ποτ’ ἔστιν φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον, οὐκ ὀκνήσω λέγειν. φιλάνθρωπός ἐστιν ὁ καὶ ἐχθροὺς εὐεργετῶν. ὅτι δὲ οὕτως ἔχει, ἄκουσον. φιλανθρωπία ἐστὶν ἀρρενόθηλυς, ἧς τὸ θῆλυ μέρος ἐλεημοσύνη λέγεται, τὸ δὲ ἄρρεν αὐτῆς ἀγάπη πρὸς τὸν πλησίον ὠνόμασται· πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐστὶν ὁ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος, οὐχ ὁ τὶς ἄνθρωπος· ἄνθρωπος γὰρ ἐστιν καὶ ὁ κακὸς καὶ ὁ ἀγαθὸς καὶ ὁ ἐχθρὸς καὶ ὁ φίλος. χρὴ οὖν τὸν φιλανθρωπίαν ἀσκοῦντα μιμητὴν εἶναι τοῦ θεοῦ, εὐεργετοῦντα δικαίους καὶ ἀδίκους, ὡς αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς πᾶσιν ἐν τῷ νῦν κόσμῳ τόν τε ἥλιον καὶ τοὺς ὑετοὺς αὐτοῦ παρέχων. εἰ δὲ θέλεις ἀγαθοὺς μὲν εὐεργετεῖν, κακοὺς δὲ μηκέτι ἢ καὶ κολάζειν, κριτοῦ τὸ ἔργον ἐπιχειρεῖς πράττειν, οὐ τὸ τῆς φιλανθρωπίας σπουδάζεις ἔχειν.

κἀγὼ ἔφην Ἀρά γε καὶ ὁ θεὸς μέλλων τότε κρίνειν, ὡς διδάσκεις ἡμᾶς, οὐ φιλάνθρωπός ἐστιν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Τοὐναντίον λέγεις. ἐπεὶ γὰρ κρινεῖ, διὰ τοῦτο φιλάνθρωπός ἐστιν. φιλῶν γὰρ καὶ ἐλεῶν τοὺς ἠδικημένους τιμωρεῖ τοὺς ἠδικηκότας. κἀγὼ ἔφην Οὐκοῦν, εἰ κἀγὼ ἀγαθοὺς μὲν εὐεργετῶ, τοὺς δὲ ἀδικοῦντας καθὸ ἀνθρώπους ἠδίκησαν τιμωρῶ, φιλάνθρωπός εἰμι; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο Εἰ μετὰ τοῦ πρόγνωσιν ἔχειν εἶχες καὶ τοῦ κρίνειν ἐξουσίαν, ὀρθῶς ἂν τοῦτο ἐποίεις, διὰ μὲν τὸ εἰληφέναι τὴν ἐξουσίαν καταδικάζων οὓς ὁ θεὸς ἐδημιούργησεν, διὰ δὲ τὴν πρόγνωσιν ἀπταίστως ἐν τῷ κρίνειν οὓς μὲν ὡς δικαίους δικαιῶν, οὓς δὲ ὡς ἀδίκους καταδικάζων. κἀγὼ ἔφην Ὀρθῶς ἔφης καὶ ἀληθῶς· ἀδύνατον γάρ τινὰ πρόγνωσιν οὐκ ἔχοντα ὀρθῶς κρῖναι. ἐνίοτε γὰρ φαίνονταί τινες ἀγαθοί, ἀθέμιτα κρύφα διαπρασσόμενοι, ἔνιοι δὲ ἀγαθοὶ ὑπὸ διαβολῆς ἐχθρῶν κακοὶ ὑπολαμβανόμενοι. ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ τοῦ βασανίζειν καὶ ἀνακρίνειν ἐξουσίαν τις ἔχων δικάζει, οὐδὲ οὕτως τὸ πάντως δικαίως αὐτῷ δικάσαι ἐγίνετο. ἔνιοι γὰρ φονεῖς ὄντες τὰς βασάνους ὑπομείναντες ὡς ἀθῷοι ἀπελύθησαν, ἕτεροι δὲ ἀθῷοι ὄντες τὰς βασάνους μὴ ὑπομείναντες, ἑαυτῶν καταψευσάμενοι ὡς αἴτιοι ἐκολάσθησαν.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Μετρίως, ἔφη, ἔχει καὶ ταῦτα, τὸ δὲ μεῖζον ἄκουσον. ἐνίων ἀνθρώπων ἁμαρτανόντων ἢ εὖ πραττόντων, ὧν νῦν ποιοῦσιν ἃ μὲν ἴδια αὐτῶν ἐστίν, ἃ δὲ ἀλλότρια, δίκαιον δὲ ἕκαστον ἐπὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις ἁμαρτήμασιν τιμωρεῖσθαι ἢ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις κατορθώμασιν εὐεργετεῖσθαι. ἀδύνατον δὲ τινὶ πλὴν προφήτῃ μόνῳ πρόγνωσιν ἔχοντι τὰ ὑπὸ τινὸς γινόμενα εἰδέναι ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν· πάντα γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ γινόμενα βλέπεται. κἀγὼ ἔφην Ἐβουλόμην μαθεῖν πῶς τῶν ἀδικημάτων ἢ κατορθωμάτων ἃ μὲν ἴδια, ἃ δὲ ἀλλότρια.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο ὅτι Ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας προφήτης ἔφη „τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐλθεῖν δεῖ, μακάριος δὲ (φησίν) δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται· ὁμοίως καὶ τὰ κακὰ ἀνάγκη ἐλθεῖν, οὐαὶ δὲ δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται“. εἰ δὲ διὰ κακῶν κακὰ ἔρχεται·καὶ δι’ ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθὰ φέρεται, προσεῖναι δεῖ ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἴδιον (τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι ἢ κακόν) καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν, διὰ τοῦ ἐλθεῖν τὰ δεύτερα ἀγαθὰ ἢ κακά, ἅτινα ἴδια αὐτοῦ τῆς αἱρέσεως ὄντα ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ προνοίας διελθεῖν ᾠκονόμηται. ἐπεὶ οὖν κρίσις αὕτη θεῷ, ὥσπερ ἐπ᾽ ἀγῶνος τὸν διὰ πάσης κακουχίας διεληλυθότα καὶ ἄμεμπτον εὑρεθέντα, ἐκεῖνον ζωῆς αἰωνίου καταξιοῦσθαι —· οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες; ὑπὸ τῶν ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ ἐν κακίᾳ παραμεινάντων πειράζονται, διωκόμενοι, μισούμενοι, λοιδορούμενοι, ἐπιβουλευόμενοι, τυπτόμενοι, πλεονεκτούμενοι, διαβαλλόμενοι, ἀγγαρευόμενοι, ἐπηρεαζόμενοι, πάντα ἐκεῖνα πάσχοντες, δι᾽ ὧν εὐλόγως δοκεῖ τὸ ὀργίζεσθαι γίνεσθαι καὶ πρὸς ἄμυναν ὁρμᾶν.

ὁ δὲ διδάσκαλος εἰδὼς ὅτι οἱ ταῦτα ἀδίκως ποιοῦντες ἐκ προτέρων ἁμαρτημάτων κατάδικοί εἰσιν καὶ ὅτι διὰ καταδίκων τὸ τῆς κακίας πνεῦμα ταῦτα ἐνεργεῖ, τοὺς μὲν ἀνθρώπους καθὰ ἄνθρωποί εἰσιν, καὶ δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας ὄργανα γινομένους κακίας ἐλεεῖν συνεβούλευσεν, ὡς φιλανθρωπίαν ἀσκοῦσιν, καὶ τὸ ὅσον ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐστίν, ἀδικουμένους καὶ ἀπολύειν τῆς καταδίκης τοὺς ἀδικοῦντας, ἵνα ὥσπερ οἱ νήφοντες τοῖς μεθύουσιν βοηθῶσιν, εὐχαῖς, νηστείαις, εὐλογίαις, μὴ ἀνθιστάμενοι, μὴ ἀμυνόμενοι, ἵνα μὴ ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖον αὐτοὺς ἁμαρτεῖν ἀναγκάσωσιν. τοῦ γὰρ παθεῖν πάντως κεκριμένου τινί, οὐκ εὔλογον ἀγανακτεῖν ἐκείνῳ, δι᾽ οὗ τὸ παθεῖν γίνεται, λογισάμενον ὅτι εἰ καὶ ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἐκακούχησεν αὐτόν, διὰ τὸ πάντως κακουχηθῆναι μέλλειν διὰ ἑτέρου τὸ παθεῖν ἦν. τί οὖν ἀγανακτῶ τῷ διαθεμένῳ, ἐμοῦ πάντως παθεῖν κεκριμένου; ἀλλ᾽ ἔτι μὴν εἰ τὰ αὐτὰ τοῖς κακοῖς προφάσει ἀμύνης ποιῶμεν, παρὰ τὸ πρῶτοι δεύτεροι τὸ αὐτὸ τοῖς κακοῖς οἱ ἀγαθοὶ πράσσομεν. καὶ (ὡς ἔφην) οὐ χρὴ ἀγανακτεῖν ὡς εἰδότα ὅτι θεοῦ προνοίᾳ οἱ κακοὶ τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς τιμωροῦσιν. οἱ οὖν τοῖς τιμωροῦσιν χαλεπαίνοντες ὡς τοὺς ἀποστόλους θεοῦ ὑβρίζοντες ἁμαρτάνουσιν, τιμῶντες δὲ καὶ τὰ ἐναντία τοῖς ἀδικεῖν νομιζομένοις διατιθέμενοι αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸν θεὸν τὸν οὕτω βουλευσάμενον εὐσεβοῦσιν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: And I answered, “Does it not seem to you, then, that even the innkeeper is humane, since she did good to a woman who was a stranger and whom she did not know?” Peter said, “I know that I can call her merciful, but I do not dare call her humane, since I would not even call a mother child-loving; for she has been persuaded by labor pains and upbringing to cherish her child. Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the person who shows mercy is flattered by misfortune. Nevertheless, the merciful person is close to the humane person, because he is persuaded to do good without hunting to receive anything. At least in this way he is humane.” And I said, “By what actions, then, can someone be humane?” Peter answered, “Since I see that you are eager to hear what an act of humaneness actually is, I will not hesitate to tell you. The humane person is one who does good even to enemies. Hear why this is so. Humaneness is male-and-female: its female part is called mercy, while its male part has been named love toward one’s neighbor. Every human being is a human being’s neighbor, not merely some particular human being; for the evil person and the good person, the enemy and the friend, are all human beings. Therefore, the person who practices humaneness must be an imitator of God, doing good to the righteous and the unrighteous, just as God himself provides everyone in the present world with both his sun and his rains. But if you wish to do good to good people, but no longer to evil people, or even to punish them, you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess the work of humaneness.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φιλάνθρωπος
lexical_decisions.chosen: humane
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes active benevolence toward human beings. “Humane” maintains its connection with the recurring noun rendered “humaneness” without narrowing it to institutional philanthropy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν φιλότεκνον
lexical_decisions.chosen: I would not even call a mother child-loving
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb “call” is carried forward from εἰπεῖν and λέγειν. More literally, τὴν τεκοῦσαν is “the woman who gave birth.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς καὶ ὁ ἐρῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συνηθείας κολακεύεται καὶ εὐνῆς καὶ ὁ φίλος ὑπὸ τῆς ἀμοιβῆς: οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἐλεῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συμφορᾶς.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the person who shows mercy is flattered by misfortune.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The predicate κολακεύεται is understood elliptically in all three members of the analogy. Its unusual image of being flattered or enticed is therefore retained throughout rather than weakened in the final member.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄνευ τοῦ τι θηρᾶσθαι λαβεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: without hunting to receive anything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s hunting image and the idea of seeking some return.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φιλανθρωπία ἐστὶν ἀρρενόθηλυς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Humaneness is male-and-female
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound ἀρρενόθηλυς explicitly combines male and female. The striking image is preserved rather than reduced to “twofold”; “androgynous” would be another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ θῆλυ μέρος ἐλεημοσύνη λέγεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: its female part is called mercy
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this context ἐλεημοσύνη continues the discussion of showing mercy. “Almsgiving” is possible in other contexts but would be too narrow here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐστὶν ὁ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος, οὐχ ὁ τὶς ἄνθρωπος
lexical_decisions.chosen: Every human being is a human being’s neighbor, not merely some particular human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the contrast between every human being and a neighbor restricted to some particular person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κριτοῦ τὸ ἔργον ἐπιχειρεῖς πράττειν, οὐ τὸ τῆς φιλανθρωπίας σπουδάζεις ἔχειν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess the work of humaneness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The second τὸ is taken elliptically with ἔργον carried forward, preserving the parallel between a judge’s work and the work of humaneness. It could more generally mean “what belongs to humaneness,” including the quality itself.

passages.text: And I said, “Surely God too, since he is going to judge then, as you teach us, is not humane?” Peter replied, “You are saying the opposite. For it is precisely because he will judge that he is humane. In loving and showing mercy to those who have been wronged, he punishes those who wronged them.” And I said, “Therefore, if I too do good to good people but punish those who commit injustice insofar as they have wronged human beings, am I humane?” Peter answered, “If, along with possessing foreknowledge, you also possessed authority to judge, you would rightly do this: on account of having received the authority, you would condemn those whom God created; and because of your foreknowledge, you would judge without error, acquitting some as righteous and condemning others as unrighteous.” And I said, “You have spoken correctly and truthfully, for it is impossible for someone who lacks foreknowledge to judge correctly. Sometimes some people appear good while secretly committing unlawful acts, while some good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander. But even if someone possesses authority to torture and interrogate and then judges, it would not even so be possible for him to judge justly in every case. For some who were murderers endured the tortures and were released as innocent, while others who were innocent did not endure the tortures, falsely testified against themselves as guilty, and were punished.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Τοὐναντίον λέγεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: You are saying the opposite
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression directly reverses Clement’s inference and does not require an expanded theological explanation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καθὸ ἀνθρώπους ἠδίκησαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: insofar as they have wronged human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνθρώπους is read as the object of ἠδίκησαν, while καθό marks the respect or extent in which punishment is contemplated. Another possible rendering is “because they wronged human beings.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ μὲν τὸ εἰληφέναι τὴν ἐξουσίαν καταδικάζων οὓς ὁ θεὸς ἐδημιούργησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: on account of having received the authority, you would condemn those whom God created
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle καταδικάζων describes the exercise of the hypothetical authority. The striking reference to condemning people created by God is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὓς μὲν ὡς δικαίους δικαιῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: acquitting some as righteous
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this judicial context δικαιόω denotes declaring righteous or acquitting rather than making someone morally righteous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνίοτε γὰρ φαίνονταί τινες ἀγαθοί, ἀθέμιτα κρύφα διαπρασσόμενοι, ἔνιοι δὲ ἀγαθοὶ ὑπὸ διαβολῆς ἐχθρῶν κακοὶ ὑπολαμβανόμενοι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Sometimes some people appear good while secretly committing unlawful acts, while some good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first ἐνίοτε is temporal, “sometimes,” but the second expression is ἔνιοι, “some people.” The translation therefore contrasts two groups rather than introducing an unsupported second temporal category.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲ οὕτως τὸ πάντως δικαίως αὐτῷ δικάσαι ἐγίνετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: it would not even so be possible for him to judge justly in every case
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως is understood distributively in light of the contrasting examples that follow. “To judge altogether justly” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑαυτῶν καταψευσάμενοι ὡς αἴτιοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: falsely testified against themselves as guilty
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive construction denotes making a false accusation or testimony against oneself, while αἴτιοι denotes culpability or guilt.

passages.text: And Peter said, “These points too are moderately sound, but hear the greater point. When some people sin or act well, among the things they now do some are their own and others belong to someone else; yet it is just for each person to be punished for his own sins or benefited for his own right actions. But it is impossible for anyone except a prophet alone, who possesses foreknowledge, to know which of the things done by someone are his own and which were not his own; for everything is seen to happen through him.” And I said, “I would like to learn how, among acts of injustice or right actions, some are one’s own and others belong to someone else.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Μετρίως, ἔφη, ἔχει καὶ ταῦτα
lexical_decisions.chosen: These points too are moderately sound
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετρίως gives qualified approval rather than complete endorsement. “These things too are reasonable to a degree” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἃ μὲν ἴδια αὐτῶν ἐστίν, ἃ δὲ ἀλλότρια
lexical_decisions.chosen: some are their own and others belong to someone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδια and ἀλλότρια contrast actions attributable to the person with actions whose agency or ownership belongs elsewhere.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις κατορθώμασιν εὐεργετεῖσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: benefited for his own right actions
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατόρθωμα denotes a right, successful, or virtuous action. “Achievement” is possible but could obscure the moral contrast with sins.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν προφήτῃ μόνῳ πρόγνωσιν ἔχοντι
lexical_decisions.chosen: except a prophet alone, who possesses foreknowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the exception marked by πλήν and the exclusivity expressed by μόνῳ are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: which ... are his own and which were not his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the supplied shift from present ἐστιν to past ἦν while supplying “his own” in the second member from the first. Regularizing ἦν to a present tense would require emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντα γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ γινόμενα βλέπεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: for everything is seen to happen through him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participial phrase is taken predicatively with βλέπεται: all the actions appear to occur through the person, even though only a prophet can discern which are truly the person’s own. It could also be construed as “everything that happens through him is seen.”

source_issues.source_quote: ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν
source_issues.issue: The printed comma after ποῖά is editorially awkward, and the shift from present ἐστιν to past ἦν is abrupt. The supplied wording nevertheless permits a defensible translation without changing the Greek.

passages.text: And Peter answered, “The prophet of truth said, ‘The good things must come; but blessed (he says) is the one through whom they come. Likewise, the evil things must necessarily come; but woe to the one through whom they come.’ Now if evil things come through evil people and good things are borne through good people, what is each person’s own—being good or evil—must also belong to him on the basis of the things he did beforehand, through the coming of the subsequent good or evil things. These, being his own as matters of choice, have been arranged by God’s providence to pass through him. God’s judgment, then, is this: just as in a contest, the one who has passed through every hardship and been found blameless is to be deemed worthy of eternal life. For those who, by their own resolve, have come to the fore in good things are tested by those who, by their own resolve, have persisted in evil: they are persecuted, hated, reviled, plotted against, beaten, exploited, slandered, pressed into service, and abused, suffering all those things through which becoming angry and rushing toward retaliation seem reasonably to arise.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐλθεῖν δεῖ, μακάριος δὲ (φησίν) δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: The good things must come; but blessed (he says) is the one through whom they come
lexical_decisions.rationale: The positive form of the saying is translated as supplied rather than harmonized with a familiar parallel, and the separate parenthetical attribution φησίν is explicitly retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κακὰ ἀνάγκη ἐλθεῖν, οὐαὶ δὲ δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil things must necessarily come; but woe to the one through whom they come
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνάγκη expresses necessity. The singular Greek verb treats the neuter plural collectively, while idiomatic English uses a plural verb.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προσεῖναι δεῖ ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἴδιον (τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι ἢ κακόν) καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: what is each person’s own—being good or evil—must also belong to him on the basis of the things he did beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The parenthesis identifies what is proper to the person as being good or evil. The compressed καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν is taken as identifying the basis supplied by prior conduct; it could alternatively mean that the person’s character is known from what he previously did.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα ἴδια αὐτοῦ τῆς αἱρέσεως ὄντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: These, being his own as matters of choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: αἵρεσις is understood as personal choice or resolve. The compact genitive construction could also be represented as “belonging to his own choice.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ προνοίας διελθεῖν ᾠκονόμηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: have been arranged by God’s providence to pass through him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject is the preceding good or evil things. “Through him” is contextually supplied from the repeated description of events coming through good or evil agents; a less agent-focused alternative is “have been arranged by God’s providence to run their course.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ οὖν κρίσις αὕτη θεῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s judgment, then, is this
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed nominal clause introduces the content expressed by the following accusative-and-infinitive construction. More formally, it could be rendered “For this, then, is judgment with God” or “Since this judgment belongs to God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: For those who, by their own resolve, have come to the fore in good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering follows the supplied προκύψαντες from προκύπτω, conveying emergence or coming forward. It does not silently substitute προκόψαντες, which would more directly mean “advanced” or “made progress.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγγαρευόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: pressed into service
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being compelled to perform service or labor, so the coercive force is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ἄμυναν ὁρμᾶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: rushing toward retaliation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄμυνα can denote defense or retaliatory action. “Retaliation” fits the following warning against responding to mistreatment in kind, though “self-defense” remains possible.

source_issues.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες;
source_issues.issue: The printed Greek semicolon functions as a question mark, but the clause continues syntactically with ὑπὸ τῶν ... πειράζονται and is defensibly read as declarative. The punctuation is treated provisionally as an editorial oddity, not as evidence that wording is missing.
source_issues.proposed_reading: οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες,

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπεὶ οὖν κρίσις αὕτη θεῷ, ὥσπερ ἐπ᾽ ἀγῶνος τὸν διὰ πάσης κακουχίας διεληλυθότα καὶ ἄμεμπτον εὑρεθέντα, ἐκεῖνον ζωῆς αἰωνίου καταξιοῦσθαι —·
source_issues.issue: The construction is compressed, with a nominal statement followed by an accusative-and-infinitive formulation, and the closing dash and point are editorially unusual. The translation treats the infinitive as defining the stated judgment; this is provisional but defensible without restoring, deleting, or altering words.

passages.text: “But the Teacher, knowing that those who do these things unjustly stand condemned because of earlier sins, and that through condemned people the spirit of evil carries out these things, counseled them, as people practicing humaneness, to have mercy on human beings insofar as they are human, even though through sin they become instruments of evil. He also counseled them, as far as it lay with them, while being wronged, to release the wrongdoers from condemnation, so that, just as sober people help drunk people, they might help them with prayers, fasts, and blessings, neither resisting nor retaliating, so that they would not force them to sin still more. For when suffering has in any event been decreed for someone, it is not reasonable for that person to be indignant with the one through whom the suffering comes, when he reflects that even if that person had not mistreated him, because he was in any event going to be mistreated, the suffering would have come through someone else. Why, then, am I indignant with the one who brought it about, when it has in any event been decreed that I suffer? But moreover, if on the pretext of retaliation we do the same things as evil people, then, apart from being second rather than first, we who are good do the same thing as evil people. And (as I said) one should not be indignant, knowing that by God’s providence evil people punish good people. Those, therefore, who are angry with those who punish them sin as people who insult God’s emissaries; but those who honor them and treat them with the opposite of what is considered injurious act reverently toward God, who has so resolved.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ καταδίκων τὸ τῆς κακίας πνεῦμα ταῦτα ἐνεργεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: through condemned people the spirit of evil carries out these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The condemned people are represented as intermediate agents through whom the spirit acts. The author’s claim is retained without theological harmonization.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς μὲν ἀνθρώπους καθὰ ἄνθρωποί εἰσιν, καὶ δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας ὄργανα γινομένους κακίας ἐλεεῖν συνεβούλευσεν, ὡς φιλανθρωπίαν ἀσκοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: counseled them, as people practicing humaneness, to have mercy on human beings insofar as they are human, even though through sin they become instruments of evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσκοῦσιν is read as a dative plural participle referring to the implicitly counseled hearers. κακίας is taken with ὄργανα, while δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας identifies how people become such instruments. The concessive “even though” expresses the contrast between their humanity and their instrumental role.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ὅσον ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: as far as it lay with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom limits the action to what lies within their power. “As far as depended on them” is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ οἱ νήφοντες τοῖς μεθύουσιν βοηθῶσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: just as sober people help drunk people
lexical_decisions.rationale: Because νήφοντες is explicitly contrasted with μεθύουσιν, the literal sober-versus-drunk image is retained rather than generalized to “clear-minded.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ ἀνθιστάμενοι, μὴ ἀμυνόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: neither resisting nor retaliating
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνθίστημι denotes resistance, while ἀμύνομαι can mean defending oneself or retaliating. The latter sense fits the repeated warning against returning harmful acts, though “nor defending themselves” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ γὰρ παθεῖν πάντως κεκριμένου τινί
lexical_decisions.chosen: when suffering has in any event been decreed for someone
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως is understood as expressing inevitability in this argument. The genitive construction supplies the circumstance under which indignation is declared unreasonable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τί οὖν ἀγανακτῶ τῷ διαθεμένῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Why, then, am I indignant with the one who brought it about
lexical_decisions.rationale: διατίθημι is elliptical here and refers to the person who occasioned the suffering. “The one who dealt with me this way” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ τὰ αὐτὰ τοῖς κακοῖς προφάσει ἀμύνης ποιῶμεν, παρὰ τὸ πρῶτοι δεύτεροι τὸ αὐτὸ τοῖς κακοῖς οἱ ἀγαθοὶ πράσσομεν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: if on the pretext of retaliation we do the same things as evil people, then, apart from being second rather than first, we who are good do the same thing as evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The datives τοῖς κακοῖς are comparative with τὰ αὐτά and τὸ αὐτό: the good do the same things as the evil, rather than doing those things to evil people. The compressed πρῶτοι δεύτεροι contrasts initiating the conduct with repeating it in response.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς τοὺς ἀποστόλους θεοῦ ὑβρίζοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: as people who insult God’s emissaries
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόστολοι is used generically for people functioning as sent agents, not necessarily for holders of the particular apostolic office. “Messengers” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τιμῶντες δὲ καὶ τὰ ἐναντία τοῖς ἀδικεῖν νομιζομένοις διατιθέμενοι αὐτοὺς
lexical_decisions.chosen: but those who honor them and treat them with the opposite of what is considered injurious
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῖς ... νομιζομένοις is taken as neuter, referring to things considered injurious, which supplies a defensible comparison without adding a customary way in which wrongdoers are treated. A masculine construal is possible—“treating them in ways opposite to those regarded as doing wrong”—but leaves the exact relation of the comparison more compressed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν θεὸν τὸν οὕτω βουλευσάμενον εὐσεβοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: act reverently toward God, who has so resolved
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐσεβέω denotes reverent or pious conduct toward God. βουλεύομαι is understood as resolving or determining the providential arrangement; “who has planned it this way” is also possible.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
